Two sides share the work: an assessor lists and values property, and a collector bills and collects. Both sit at 913 Greensboro Street, 3rd Floor, Suite 303, Lexington (NC 27292), open weekdays 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM. A second counter in Denton opens at 8:30 AM on weekdays.

  • Tax office and appeals line: 336-242-2160.
  • Collections line: 336-242-2180.
  • Assessor mailing address: P.O. Box 1617, Lexington, NC 27293.
  • Payment mailing address: Davidson County Tax Collector, P.O. Box 1577, Lexington, NC 27293.

The assessor's side answers questions on listing, billing and assessed values. The collector's job stops at collecting.

About 180,182 people live in the county, in 69,846 households, and 74.4 percent of those households own. The median owned home is valued at $219,100, and the median household income is $64,172 (2024 dollars).

The county's own rate is 0.5400 on the 2026 sheet. A parcel inside a city, school district or fire district picks up that jurisdiction's rate as well. Call the tax office to confirm the final numbers for your parcel.

Fire districts are listed separately and run from 0.0965 for Reeds Fire to 0.1624 for Healing Springs Fire. City motor vehicle fees are $30.00 in Lexington and High Point, $20.00 in Thomasville and $5.00 in Denton. Discounts do not apply to the city and municipal service district lines.

Each July the county mails bills for land, buildings and business or personal property. September 1 is the due date, and interest waits until after January 5. A January 5 that falls on a weekend rolls to the next business day.

Early payers save: 1 1/2 percent off in July, 1 percent off in August. A postmark of January 5 is on time, but the county advises sending it a week ahead. Once an account is past due, 2 percent is added for January and 3/4 percent more for every month after. If you need a payment plan, arrange it when the annual bill lands and finish it by the delinquent date. The office takes cards.

Values last reset on January 1, 2021. The reappraisal once planned for 2026 now falls in 2027 under new legislation. State law requires counties to reappraise at least once every eight years, and a revaluation here covers more than 97,000 parcels.

The aim is to equalize values, not to raise revenue, and elected officials set the rates in June. If you appealed a 2026 or 2027 value on time, you do not need to refile, and any change from those appeals applies to the 2027 tax year. The county's appeal page has separate forms for the current 2026 value and the 2027 revaluation value, and questions can go to revalhelp@davidsoncountync.gov.

Appeals run on three levels. You begin with an informal review, where a county appraiser reads your property record and looks at whatever evidence you bring. A mistake found there is corrected with no formal appeal.

Next is a formal hearing before the Board of Equalization and Review. By law the commissioners sit as that board unless a special one is created, and Davidson County describes its board as local residents with real estate knowledge, appointed by the commissioners. After an unwelcome board decision, you can give written notice to the state Property Tax Commission, and the 30 days run from the date the board's notice is mailed.

The county lists reasons that are not grounds for a reduction:

  • The size of the percentage increase or decrease.
  • A market value above the insurance value.
  • A feeling that the value is simply too high.
  • An owner's inability to pay the tax.

North Carolina sets up three relief programs, and you may claim just one of them. Older or permanently disabled owners with income of $38,800 or less (2026) can exclude $25,000 or half the appraised value, whichever is larger.

Under the circuit breaker, a household at or below that income limit pays no more than 4.0 percent of income, and one up to 150 percent of the limit ($58,200 for 2026) pays no more than 5.0 percent. Five years as owner and occupant come first. The disabled veteran exclusion is the third: $45,000 off the value, whatever the owner's age or income.

Form AV-9 goes to the county assessor, and the homestead application is linked from the property information page on the county site. Any tax deferred by the circuit breaker turns into a lien that must be paid when title transfers, so a sale triggers it.

Interest starts after the January 5 deadline, and the bill then becomes subject to collection. The collector can use wage garnishment, attachment of bank accounts or rents, levy on personal property and, for real estate, foreclosure by sale at public auction.

  • Unpaid real estate accounts can be advertised in local newspapers from March 1 to June 30, at added cost to the taxpayer.
  • Sheriff's warrants, in rem foreclosures and attachment of the state tax refund are also used.
  • The lien date is the listing date under state law, so the lien exists before the bill is due.

The county posts a PDF list of 2025 delinquent taxpayers and a tax foreclosure list. Davidson County also requires a tax certificate before the Register of Deeds takes a deed, so a delinquent balance has to be cleared first.

A mid-year sale leaves the January 1 owner on the hook for that year's bill. Find out whether the closing will prorate it. The tidiest route is for the closing attorney to pay the collector directly out of your proceeds.

With no attorney closing, ask for the tax certificate well ahead of time, because the deed will be turned away at the Register of Deeds without it. Check any open 2026 or 2027 appeal as well, since a changed value takes effect for 2027.

Before listing, pull together your latest bill, proof of any exclusion and a payoff figure from the collections line, 336-242-2180. A cash buyer does not wait on a lender, which helps when a delinquent balance or newspaper advertising is running. Whatever the buyer's financing, the taxes come out of the sale money first.

faqs.q: When do Davidson County property taxes come due?
faqs.a: September 1, and no interest accrues through January 5. Paying in July saves 1 1/2 percent, and paying in August saves 1 percent.

faqs.q: What rate applies to a Davidson County home?
faqs.a: The county's 2026 rate is 0.5400, plus any city, school and fire district rates. Lexington is 0.6500 and Thomasville is 0.6200. The tax office can confirm the final rate for your address.

faqs.q: Did Davidson County delay its revaluation?
faqs.a: Yes, the 2026 revaluation moved to 2027 under new legislation. Timely appeals of 2026 or 2027 values still get reviewed, and a change applies for the 2027 tax year.

faqs.q: How do I challenge my Davidson County assessment?
faqs.a: Submit the county's form for an informal sit-down with an appraiser. If that does not settle it, a formal hearing follows, and a further appeal to the state Property Tax Commission is due within 30 days of the board's mailing.

faqs.q: How much interest do late Davidson County taxes carry?
faqs.a: Past-due real estate is charged 2 percent for January and 3/4 percent per month afterward. Send payments by mail at least five business days before January 5.
